I have farmed these fields in Quzhou County for more than forty years. I am sixty-seven now, and I know every inch of my land. I hold six mu of good flat plots near the village. At my age, with my middle school education, I do not chase after risky new crops like some of the younger folks do. I stick to the double cropping system that has always fed my family and given me a reliable cash income: winter wheat followed by summer maize. It is what the land and the climate of the North China Plain are made for.

This autumn I will sow improved winter wheat again—probably a Jimai variety that the county station recommends, because it stands up well to lodging and the cold. I will prepare the seedbed with rotary tillage, the same way I have done for years. For the wheat crop, I will apply about eighteen kilograms of nitrogen, seven kilograms of phosphorus, and five kilograms of potassium per mu. The wheat needs three good irrigations: one before winter to protect the roots from freezing, one at jointing when the weather warms, and a final one during grain filling in May. I will spray herbicide once in early spring, and if aphids or rust show up, I will add insecticide and fungicide, so probably three or four sprayings in total.

After I harvest the wheat in early June—usually around the fifth or sixth—I will immediately plant hybrid summer maize. I have been using Denghai 605 seed for several years now; it is a good hybrid that yields well and the seed dealer in town always has it in stock. For maize, I use no-tillage planting right into the wheat stubble. It saves me precious days during the busy summer and keeps the soil moisture in. The maize will get about fifteen kilograms of nitrogen, five kilograms of phosphorus, and four kilograms of potassium per mu. Summer rainfall usually helps, but if July turns dry, I will irrigate twice—once during the rapid growth stage and once at flowering. I will control weeds and watch for armyworms, spraying two or three times as needed.

I expect the wheat to yield around 550 kilograms per mu, and the maize should reach about 600 kilograms per mu if the weather cooperates. I thought about renting in more land or trying vegetables, but at sixty-seven I do not want the extra labor or market uncertainty. Wheat and maize are safe, the grain buyers come to the village, and I can manage the work with occasional hired help at harvest.
